sentences.text: The Rodrigues parrot, scientifically named Necropsittacus rodricanus, was an extinct parrot species that lived only on the island of Rodrigues. It was the largest parrot species found on that island, distinguished by its large head and long tail.
Contemporary accounts describe the bird's plumage as having a uniform green coloration.
To escape introduced rats, this parrot frequented and nested on offshore islets where these predators were absent.
By 1671, the bird had already become rare and was considered popular game by local hunters.
The species was first mentioned by French traveler François Leguat in his 1708 memoir, A New Voyage to the East Indies.

In 1867, French zoologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards described subfossil bones of the Rodrigues parrot received via British ornithologist Alfred Newton. He scientifically named the species Psittacus rodricanus based on a fragmentary upper beak.
By 1873, Milne-Edwards moved the species to the genus Necropsittacus after receiving more complete beak remains.
Subfossil remains of the bird have been found in caves on the Plaine Corail and in Caverne Tortue.
The Rodrigues parrot is classified as a member of the tribe Psittaculini, though its closest relative among other species remains unclear.
The genus Necropsittacus was established by Milne-Edwards in 1874, while the specific species Necropsittacus rodricanus was originally described by him in 1867.
The genus Necropsittacus lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.

The Rodrigues parrot was last mentioned in 1761 and likely went extinct soon after due to introduced predators, deforestation, and human hunting. Julian Hume suggested in 2007 that Leguat's mention of green and blue parrots could refer to both the Rodrigues parrot and Newton's parakeet, or represent color morphs of the parakeet. Samuel Pasfield Oliver doubted in 1891 that the parrots mentioned by Leguat were the Rodrigues parrot, suggesting they were actually Newton's parakeet due to size differences.

In 1893, E. Newton and Hans Gadow found the Rodrigues parrot closely related to the broad-billed parrot but could not determine if they belonged in the same genus due to missing crest evidence. Graham S. Cowles found the skulls of the Rodrigues parrot and broad-billed parrot too dissimilar to be close relatives in 1987.

In 1967, ornithologist James Greenway suggested that the species N. borbonicus might have been an escaped pet lory rather than a wild bird. In 2007, Hume suggested that Rothschild mistakenly linked N. borbonicus to the Rodrigues parrot by incorporating Dubois's account into the latter's description.
